A1.justification: Both PDFs clearly describe DRAMA, and their supplied text, equations, figures and tables are readable. Neither contains an appendix. However, v2 refers to supplementary predictor details, dataset specifications and full ablation results that are not included, limiting comparison of those materials.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulation experiments comparing coordination methods, repeated-run stability results and backbone-model evaluations in Figures 3-4 and Table 2.

after.justification: v2 reports original simulation comparisons, stability distributions, backbone evaluations and component ablations in Tables 1-4 and Figure 3.

M1.justification: v1's centralized Monitor/Planner-Critic architecture becomes a three-layer system using Dual-Capacity Hungarian Assignment, ordered guardian chains for decentralized takeover, and an MLP-based shared spatial predictor. These change allocation, recovery and navigation procedures; existing hierarchical memory and local task planning are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use C-WAH-derived household tasks in VirtualHome-Social. Beyond that retained environment, v2 adds cascading population changes, recovery at the original location and replacement by a new agent elsewhere (Section 4.4, Table 1). It also reports increasing task-type diversity, whereas v1 describes increasing object counts.

E2.justification: The evaluated external comparators remain CoELA, MCTS, ProAgent, AgentVerse-Static and AgentVerse-Dynamic. Both versions omit MCTS from their repeated-run stability plots. The new component-removal variants are ablations.

E3.justification: Static configurations change from 2/3/4 to 3/4/5 agents, and dynamic events move from random steps 5-10 to fixed execution-progress ratios. CR and TP replace TS and numerical SR reporting alongside AS. Stability evaluation changes from two tasks to one complex task. The backbone tables change DeepSeek-V3 to DeepSeek-V3.2.

E4.justification: v2 adds Collective Intelligence Layer and Trust Chain ablations, measuring their contributions to efficiency, conflicts and throughput (Section 5.5, Table 4). It revises stability testing for cascading population changes and removes v1's illustrated dropout case study and Figure 5.

E5.justification: The stability study's reported independent-run count decreases from 100 to 50 (v1 Figure 4; v2 Figure 3). Both retain empirical distribution plots; neither introduces seed lists, confidence intervals or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: v1's AS/TS results and SR/AS/TS backbone table are replaced by extensive AS/CR/TP results, revised backbone scores and new ablation outcomes in v2 Tables 1, 3 and 4. Table 2 adds recovery success. For example, v2 reports DRAMA's 4-to-3 dropout results as AS 57.205, CR 0.026 and TP 0.200. Changed methods and settings preclude interpreting these as same-setting gains over v1.

T1.justification: v1's generic resource-state and Scheduler/Planner-Critic formulations are replaced by explicit weighted affinity, constrained total-affinity maximization, guardian ordering and spatial-probability definitions in v2 Sections 3.1-3.2. This substantially revises the mathematical model, although neither version supplies theoretical proofs.

C1.justification: The principal contribution shifts from control/worker-plane allocation to embodied three-layer orchestration with shared spatial reasoning and trust-chain recovery. The uniqueness claim expands from dropout support to dropout and recovery. The abstract changes its headline from 17% runtime improvement and 13% resource reduction to 7% runtime improvement and 10% throughput improvement; v2's introduction still claims 17% runtime improvement.

C2.justification: v2 newly attributes efficiency mainly to collective spatial intelligence and robustness mainly to the Trust Chain, supported by its ablation discussion. It adds an explanation for MCTS's lower conflict rates. v1's limitations concerning centralized failure, scalability and LLM-affinity latency disappear; v2 instead explicitly states a five-agent implementation limit.

D1.justification: Visible additions include DCHA pseudocode specifying virtual slots and cost-matrix construction, pooled observation histories, predictor inputs/outputs, simulator-failure reruns and the five-agent capacity limit. Neither supplied PDF provides code access, hardware specifications or detailed training hyperparameters. Further predictor and dataset details referenced by v2 are unavailable.

R1.justification: v2 expands embodied-agent positioning with works on embodied reasoning, task-and-motion planning, MP5 and an EMAS review, and adds dynamic Hungarian and drone-scheduling references. It removes Agent-oriented planning in multi-agent systems. Most existing LLM-MAS literature and baseline positioning remain.

P1.justification: The title and DRAMA expansion change, and the abstract, introduction, methodology and results narrative are extensively rewritten. Method exposition is reorganized into three named layers with numbered sections. The case-study and limitations sections disappear, an ablation subsection and acknowledgment appear, and the author/affiliation block changes.

P2.justification: Figures 1-2 are substantially redrawn. v1's efficiency bar chart becomes v2's full-width results table, the stability display expands from four to six panels, the case-study figure disappears, and an ablation table is added. Table styling, captions, headings and page layout also change extensively.

improvement.justification: v2 improves procedural specificity and adds component ablations and recovery/replacement tests, addressing important evidential gaps in v1. However, Equation 5's one-to-one constraint conflicts with Algorithm 1's two-task capacity, and the claim of highest throughput in every scenario contradicts Table 1: recovery TP is 0.204 for DRAMA versus 0.214 for ProAgent. Missing supplementary predictor/data details further limit reproducibility assessment. These benefits and unresolved problems prevent a reliable net-quality judgment.
